title.en: The Origin of Death: The Twins' Unfinished Argument
title.zh: 死亡之始：雙生子未完之辯

region.zh: 柯達倫村落屋內（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 14. Origin of Death'

summary.en: A woman leaves her twin children, who seem to faint away (or only sleep); she notices tracks like theirs around the house and thinks they come to life and play in her absence. One day she steals on them unseen and finds them arguing inside the lodge — one says, 'It is better to be dead,' the other, 'It is better to be alive.' When they saw her they stopped talking; and since then people die from time to time, always some being born and some dying, some living ones and some dead ones. Had she remained hidden and allowed them to finish their argument, one would have prevailed over the other, and there would have been either no life or no death.
summary.zh: 一婦人晨出暮歸，其雙生子女終日昏睡（或云實乃假寐）。她見屋周有其足跡，疑其醒時嬉戲。一日她悄然而入，竟聞二子於屋內爭論：一言『死勝於生』，一言『生勝於死』。二子見母，言止。自此人乃有生死之別，生者死者並存於世。若婦人隱而不出，任其辯畢，則其一必勝——世間將或有生無死，或有死無生。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Origin-of-death cluster (interrupted-debate variant). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once a woman had twin children (some say brother and sister) who fainted away; possibly they only slept. Their mother left them in the morning; and when she returned in the evening, they were still lying there. She noticed tracks like theirs around the house: therefore she thought they must come to life and play during her absence. One day she stole on them unseen, and found them arguing with each other inside the lodge. One said, 'It is better to be dead'; and the other said, 'It is better to be alive.' When they saw her, they stopped talking; and since then people die from time to time. There are always some being born and some dying at the same time, always some living ones and some dead ones. Had she remained hidden, and allowed them to finish their argument, one would have prevailed over the other, and there would have been either no life or no death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 125 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.zh: 庫茲庫茲特：獾拐郊狼之子

region.en: Star group probably the Pleiades and two stars near them (symbolic pin at Coeur d'Alene)
region.zh: 星群，疑為昴星團及其附近雙星（象徵定位於柯達倫）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 15. Star Myths, (1) Qo'zqozt'

summary.en: Once Badger stole Coyote's favorite child, and Coyote chased them; as he was nearly overtaking them, they became transformed into stars — a group probably the Pleiades and two stars near them, which the Thompson consider a group of people, some saying they are Coyote's children. Coyote thus lost his child, and the group of people who were looking on were also transformed into stars.
summary.zh: 獾拐走郊狼最寵愛的孩子，郊狼窮追不捨；追及之際，三者俱化為星辰——即昴星團附近之星群（湯普森人謂其為一群人，或云郊狼之子）。郊狼自此失子；圍觀之眾亦化為星。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene star-myth recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. The pin is symbolic (the sky). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once Badger stole Coyote's favorite child. Coyote chased them; and as he was nearly overtaking them, they became transformed into stars (the group Qo'zqozt, probably the Pleiades, and two stars near them; the Thompson consider the Pleiades to have been a group of people, and some say they are Coyote's children). Coyote thus lost his child. A group of people who were looking on were also transformed into stars.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 125 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.zh: 斯格威爾凱倫：煮卡瑪斯之婦

region.en: Earth oven by the camas beds (symbolic pin at Coeur d'Alene)
region.zh: 卡瑪斯田畔地灶（象徵定位於柯達倫）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 15. Star Myths, (2) sgwelkai'len'

summary.en: Some women were cooking camas in an earth oven; the roots nearly done, they sat down in a circle round the pit. Skunk went there to spoil the camas but could not reach it because the women encircled the pit, and sat down a little distance off to wait. As they were thus seated, they were transformed into stars — the group Sgwelkai'len, seemingly the large stars of Auriga and Perseus, which the Thompson call 'The Women Cooking Roots.'
summary.zh: 眾婦以地灶煮卡瑪斯根，將熟之際環灶而坐。臭鼬欲毀其根，然婦人環灶而守，無從下手，只得稍退以待。眾人坐間，俱化為星——即斯格威爾凱倫星群，疑為御夫座與英仙座之亮星；湯普森人稱之為『煮根之婦』。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene star-myth recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. The pin is symbolic (the sky). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Some women were cooking camas in an earth oven. The roots were nearly done, and the women sat down in a circle round the pit. Skunk went there to spoil the camas, but could not reach it, because the women encircled the pit; he sat down a little distance off to wait. As they were thus seated, they were transformed into stars (the group Sgwelkai'len, seemingly the large stars of Auriga and Perseus, called by the Thompson 'The Women Cooking Roots').
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 125 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Temexa'tcasqat: The Grizzly-Bear Hunt in the Sky
title.zh: 特梅夏茨卡沙特：天上獵熊

region.en: The Great Bear constellation (symbolic pin at Coeur d'Alene)
region.zh: 大熊星座（象徵定位於柯達倫）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 15. Star Myths, (3) temexa'.tcasqat'

summary.en: Three brothers had a brother-in-law who was a Grizzly Bear; the youngest brother was a good friend of the Bear, but the other two disliked him and said they would kill him. The Bear went off hunting one day, and the youngest brother was following him; the other brothers overtook them, and were about to shoot the Bear. The youngest brother called out, 'Brother-in-law, they are going to shoot you!' Just as they were in the act of shooting, they were transformed into stars — the group Temexa'tcasqat, evidently the Great Bear, called by the Thompson 'The Grizzly-Bear' or 'The Grizzly-Bear and Hunters.'
summary.zh: 三兄弟之姊夫乃灰熊；幼弟與之交好，二兄惡之，欲殺。一日熊出獵，幼弟隨行；二兄追至，正欲放箭。幼弟急呼：『姊夫，他們要射你！』眾人舉弓之際，俱化為星辰——即特梅夏茨卡沙特星群，顯為大熊座；湯普森人稱之為『灰熊』或『灰熊與獵人』。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene star-myth recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. The pin is symbolic (the sky). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Three brothers had a brother-in-law who was a Grizzly Bear. The youngest brother was a good friend of the Bear; but the other two brothers disliked him, and said they would kill him. The Bear went off hunting one day, and the youngest brother was following him. The other brothers overtook them, and were about to shoot the Bear. The youngest brother called out, 'Brother-in-law, they are going to shoot you!' Just as they were in the act of shooting, they were transformed into stars (the group Temexa'tcasqat, evidently the Great Bear, called by the Thompson 'The Grizzly-Bear' or 'The Grizzly-Bear and Hunters').
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 126 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Arrow-Chain of the Coeur d'Alene

region.en: Chain of arrows from earth to sky (symbolic pin at Coeur d'Alene)
region.zh: 自大地直達天際之箭鏈（象徵定位於柯達倫）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 16. The Arrow-Chain'

summary.en: The people wanted to go to the sky; they assembled and shot their arrows upward until an arrow reached the sky and stuck there, and then shot arrows at its nock until a chain of arrows reached down to the earth. The informants claimed this story used to be told often, but they had forgotten the details; Eagle and Coyote were mentioned in it, and they thought Coyote was the one who shot the arrow that hit the sky.
summary.zh: 世人慾登天界，聚眾向上射箭，終有一箭釘天；再續射其箭尾，箭鏈垂地乃成。相傳此事古時常有人講述，然細節已佚；據云鷹與郊狼亦在其中，而釘天之箭，當屬郊狼所射。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Details were reported forgotten by the informants. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The people wanted to go to the sky. They assembled, and shot their arrows upward. At last an arrow reached the sky, and stuck there. Then they shot arrows at the nock of this one, and gradually they formed a chain of arrows which reached down to the earth. The informants claimed this story used to be told often, but they had forgotten the details; Eagle and Coyote were mentioned in it, and they thought Coyote was the one who shot the arrow that hit the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 126 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Small lake near Cheney, Spokane territory (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斯波坎故地奇尼附近小湖（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 17. The Water-Mystery'

summary.en: A number of people were dancing at a small lake near Cheney, in Spokane territory, when they became aware of a strange smell; one of them said at once, 'That is .stsomkestci'nt.' All looked where he was looking, and saw four men standing about an equal distance apart from each other, all wearing buffalo-skins around the shoulders, hair-side out, each with his hair done up so that it stood out to the side. As the people looked, they disappeared, and four bushes grew up where they disappeared — these bushes were there lately, and probably may still be seen.
summary.zh: 斯波坎故地奇尼附近小湖畔，眾人正舞，忽聞異香。一人即呼：『此乃 .stsomkestci'nt 也！』眾皆循其目而望，見四人分立四處，皆肩披野牛皮，毛面向外，髮束向上外揚。眾人凝視之際，四人不見，原處生出四叢灌木——此灌木近年猶在，或至今尚存。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Teit compares the Uta'mqt stories of land-mysteries and giants changing into trees. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once a number of people were dancing at a small lake near Cheney, in the territory of the Spokane. Suddenly they became aware of a strange smell; and one of them at once said, 'That is .stsomkestci'nt.' The man looked around, and all the people looked to where he was looking. They saw four men standing about an equal distance apart from each other; all wore buffalo-skins around the shoulders, hair-side out, and each had his hair done up so that it stood out to the side. As the people looked, they disappeared, and four bushes grew up where they disappeared. These bushes were there lately, and probably may still be seen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 127 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Water-Buffalo of Coeur d'Alene Lake

region.en: Coeur d'Alene Lake shore bush (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柯達倫湖畔灌木處（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 18. The Water-Buffalo'

summary.en: There was a water-mystery in Coeur d'Alene Lake with horns like a buffalo, otherwise somewhat like a buffalo. Once a man paddling his canoe along the shore in the dark found, opposite a bush growing near the shore, that his canoe stood still; he paddled hard, but the canoe would not move, and feeling along the gunwales he discovered a horn holding the canoe on each side — he knew the Water-Buffalo had caught him. He asked it to let him go, and gave it a present; at once it settled in the water, and the man paddled away. Ever afterwards people were careful to pray and make an offering at this place, the offerings being placed near the bush.
summary.zh: 柯達倫湖中有一水靈，其角如野牛，形亦近似。昔有人夜航沿湖而行，至湖畔灌木處，舟忽不動；奮力划槳，舟仍不移。以手探舷，兩側各有一角扣舟——知為水牛靈所擒。其人獻禮求釋，水牛靈遂沉入水中，舟行如常。自是行舟至此者，必祈禱獻祭於灌木之旁，以為定例。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was a water-mystery in the Coeur d'Alene Lake. It had horns like a buffalo, and is said to have been otherwise somewhat like a buffalo. Once a man was paddling his canoe along the shore in the dark. When opposite a place where a bush grows near the shore, his canoe stood still. He paddled hard, but the canoe would not move. Then he felt along the gunwales of the canoe, and discovered a horn holding the canoe on each side. He knew the Water-Buffalo had caught him. He asked him to let him go, and gave him a present; at once he settled in the water, and the man paddled away. Ever afterwards people were careful to pray, and make an offering at this place; the offerings were placed near the bush.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 127 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Lake Nka'mEmEn (Swallowing) near the head of San Joe River (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 聖喬河源頭之恩卡梅門湖（意為『吞沒』）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 19. The Nka'mEmEn Water-Mystery'

summary.en: Near the head of San Joe River is a lake called Nka'mEmEn (Swallowing): when people look at it, sticks jump out of the water. Once two brothers came out on the ridge above this lake, thirsty from hunting; the elder asked the other to bring him water, and the younger refused — 'No one goes near this lake' — until the elder said he would die without it. The younger descended, drew water quickly, ran uphill as fast as he could, and set down his bucket beside his brother before running down the other side; looking back, he saw a wave rise over the top of the ridge where his brother was and stand there for a while. When it disappeared, he went back and found his elder brother drowned.
summary.zh: 聖喬河源頭有湖，名恩卡梅門，意為『吞沒』：人望湖時，水面即有木棍躍出。昔有兄弟二人狩獵至此嶺，渴甚；兄命弟取水，弟拒之：『無人敢近此湖。』兄曰：『不得水，吾必死。』弟遂疾下湖畔，匆匆汲水，飛奔上山，置桶於兄旁，即越嶺而逃。回首一望，見巨浪騰越山嶺，罩於兄之所在，聳立片刻而沒。弟返尋兄，兄已溺斃。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Near the head of San Joe River is a lake called Nka'mEmEn (Swallowing). When people look at it, sticks jump out of the water. Once two brothers came out on the ridge above this lake; they had been hunting, and were very thirsty. The elder brother asked the other to bring him some water. The younger brother refused, saying, 'No one goes near this lake.' The elder said, 'I shall die if water is not brought to me.' The younger then descended, drew some water quickly, and ran uphill as fast as he could; he put down his bucket alongside his brother, and ran down the other side. He looked back, and saw a wave rise over the top of the ridge where his brother was, and stand up there for a while. When it disappeared, he went back and found his elder brother drowned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 127 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Water-Mystery of the Upper San Joe River

region.en: Deep water of the upper San Joe River and a small mystery lake (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 上聖喬河深水與鄰近小靈湖（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 20. The Water-Mystery of the Upper San Joe River'

summary.en: Long ago some women were picking service-berries a long way up the San Joe River, four sisters among them; in the hot weather the sisters said they would have a swim, and seeing a large fish out in the deep water, said, 'Let us see who can reach him first!' They swam out; and when they came near, the fish went down — the sisters went down too, and were never seen again. The other women said, 'That was not a fish, it was the tongue of the water-mystery.' Shortly afterwards, some people on a nearby mountain with a small 'mystery' lake found on the shore the hair of the four sisters; they reported their find to the parents, who went and took away the hair. The people thus learned that there was a water-passage between this small lake and the river, and that it was used by the water-mystery.
summary.zh: 昔有眾女上聖喬河採莓，中有姊妹四人。天熱，姊妹戲言下水同泳；見深水處有大魚，遂呼：『且比誰先游到！』四人並進，將近之時，魚忽沉——姊妹亦隨之而沒，從此無蹤。眾女曰：『此非魚也，乃水靈之舌。』未幾，有人於鄰山小靈湖畔拾得四姊妹之髮，報於其親，其親往取之。眾人始知此小湖與大河之間有水道相通，為水靈往來之路。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: One time long ago some women were picking service-berries a long ways up the San Joe River. Four sisters were among them. It was hot weather, and the sisters said they would have a swim. They saw a large fish out in the deep water, and said, 'Let us see who can reach him first!' They swam out; and when they came near, the fish went down. The sisters also went down, and were never seen again. The other women said, 'That was not a fish, it was the tongue of the water-mystery.' Shortly afterwards some people were on a mountain near by where there is a small 'mystery' lake. There they found on the shore the hair of the four sisters; they reported their find to the parents of the sisters, who went and took away the hair. The people thus learned that there was a water-passage between this small lake and the river, and that it was used by the water-mystery.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 128 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Firewood stands of the Coeur d'Alene country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柯達倫故地拾柴之地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 21. The Rolling Head'

summary.en: A young woman gathering fire-wood, about to rise with her load, notices a man's head on her dress, which says, 'You must be my wife.' She rises, the head falls off and rolls after her, entering the lodge close behind; when she sits down it rolls onto her dress, and she takes it up to decorate it with beads. One line of beads is strung from the back of the head to the brow, and as she works another line around from ear to ear her sister comes home, angry, and tells her to let it alone; she strikes her hand to make her stop — so the beading was never finished. The head stayed with her as her husband.
summary.zh: 少女拾柴，負重將起，忽見裙上有男子之首，且言：『汝當為吾妻。』少女起身，首落而滾，緊隨其後入屋；少女坐，首又滾上裙，遂拾起以珠飾之。自後腦至額已串珠一行，正自耳至耳再串一行，其姊歸而大怒，令其罷手，並擊其手以止之——故飾珠未竟。此首遂留其身畔，以為夫。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Rolling-head motif; cf. the Thompson rolling-bowlder tale. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once there was a young woman gathering fire-wood. She made up a load, and, having attached her pack-strap to it, sat down to place it over her head. As she was about to rise with her load, she noticed a man's head on her dress. It said to her, 'You must be my wife.' She rose up, and the head fell off her dress; she went home, and the head rolled after her. She entered the lodge, and it followed close behind her. When she sat down, it rolled on her dress. She took it up, and thought she would decorate it with beads. She had put one line of beads from the back of the head to the brow, and was engaged in putting on another line around the head from ear to ear, when her sister came home. She was angry when she saw her beading the head; she told her to let it alone, and have nothing to do with it, but the young woman kept on beading. Then her sister struck her hand to make her stop; therefore she did not finish the beading. The head stayed with her as her husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 128 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
